Winning the Auction, Losing Money

See why the winner of a coin-jar auction ends up the biggest loser.

Each bidder's guess scatters around the true value. The winner is whoever guessed the highest. More bidders means the top guess puffs up even further. Winning itself is the news that you overestimated the most. The formula below sizes that puff.

For example, a jar holds 100 🍬 candies, and 10 🧑 classmates each guess the count. One classmate guesses 130 and bids the highest, so they win. Inside are only 100, a loss equal to the 30-candy overcount.

E[top signal]=V+d⋅N−1N+1E[\text{top signal}] = V + d \cdot \frac{N-1}{N+1}E[top signal]=V+d⋅N+1N−1​
naive loss=d⋅N−1N+1\text{naive loss} = d \cdot \frac{N-1}{N+1}naive loss=d⋅N+1N−1​

Examples & Exercises

A jar of coins is truly worth 100100100.

Ten bidders each count the coins, and their signals scatter evenly within ±20\pm 20±20 of the truth.

If the winner is someone who bids exactly their own signal, how much do they lose on average?

Show proof

  1. With ten signals spread evenly, the largest one averages 100+20×911≈116.4100 + 20 \times \frac{9}{11} \approx 116.4100+20×119​≈116.4. Among that many counters, someone almost always overcounts.

  2. The winner is exactly that most optimistic bidder. Paying 116.4116.4116.4 for something worth 100100100 loses 16.416.416.4 on average — not from lack of skill, but because winning itself selects for the biggest overestimate.

  3. More bidders inflate the top signal further (at N=20N = 20N=20 the loss is 18.118.118.1). The fiercer the bidding, the deeper the naive winner's wound.

In the same jar auction (101010 bidders, spread ±20\pm 20±20), how should you fix your bid to avoid the loss?

If your signal reads sss, what should you bid?

Show proof

  1. The key is that winning itself is information. If you won, your signal was the largest of ten — and the largest signal is inflated on average.

  2. So subtract the inflation 20×911≈16.420 \times \frac{9}{11} \approx 16.420×119​≈16.4 in advance: if your signal reads sss, bid s−16.4s - 16.4s−16.4. This is arithmetic conditioned on the event of winning.

  3. Then what you pay when you win averages 100100100, and the expected loss is 000. Shade too much and you lose the auction — but that is a walk-away, not a loss.
